source_text: Resurget igitur corpus secundum christianae fidem, quae fallere non potest. quod cui uidetur incredibile, qualis nunc sit caro adtendit, qualis autem futura sit non considerat: quia illo tempore inmutationis angelicae non iam caro erit et sanguis, sed tantum corpus. cum enim de carne apostolus loqueretur, alia, inquit, caro pecorum, alia uolucrum, alia piscium, alia serpentum. et corpora caelestia, et corpora terrestria. non enim dixit: et caro caelestis, dixit autem: et caelestia et terrestria corpora. omnis enim caro etiam corpus est, non autem omne corpus etiam caro est: primo in istis terrestribus, quoniam lignum corpus est, sed non caro; hominis autem uel pecoris et corpus et caro est; in caelestibus uero nulla caro, sed corpora simplicia et lucida, quae appellat apostolus spiritalia, nonnulli autem uocant aetherea. et ideo non carnis resurrectioni contradicit illud, quod ait: caro et sanguis regnum dei non possidebunt, sed quale futurum sit, quod nunc caro et sanguis est, praedicat, in qualem naturam quisquis hanc carnem conuerti posse non credit, gradibus ducendus est ad fidem. si enim ab eo quaeras, utrum terra in aquam possit conuerti, propter uicinitatem non ei uidetur incredibile. rursus si quaeras utrum aqua possit in aerem, neque hoc absurdum esse respondet; uicina enim sunt sibi. et de aere si quaeras, utrum in aethereum corpus, id est in caeleste possit mutari, iam ipsa uicinitas persuadet. quod ergo per hos gradus fieri posse concedit, ut terra in corpus aethereum conuertatur, cur non accedente dei uoluntate, qua corpus humanum super aquas potuit ambulare, celerrime id fieri posse, quemadmodum dictum est: in ictu oculi, sine ullis talibus gradibus credit, sicut plerumque fumus in flammam mira celeritate conuertitur? caro enim nostra utique ex terra est; philosophi autem, quorum argumentis saepius resurrectioni carnis resistitur, quibus asserunt nullum esse posse terrenum corpus in caelo, omne corpus in omne corpus conuerti et mutari posse concedunt. qua corporis resurrectione facta a temporis condicione liberati aeterna uita ineffabili caritate atque stabilitate [sine corruptione] perfruemur. tunc enim fiet illud, quod scriptum est: absorta est mors in uictoria. ubi est, mors, aculeus tuus ubi est, mors, contentio tua?
thought_title: The body will rise, changed into a heavenly body
orientation: Augustine is answering objections to the resurrection of the body by arguing that the flesh will be changed into a spiritual, heavenly body.

pass_b_english: Therefore the body will rise again according to the Christian faith, which cannot deceive. To anyone who finds this incredible, it is because he pays attention to what flesh is like now and does not consider what it will be like in the future. For at that time of angelic change it will no longer be flesh and blood, but only body. When the apostle was speaking about flesh, he said: “There is one kind of flesh of cattle, another of birds, another of fish, another of snakes. And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Corinthians 15:39–40). He did not say “and heavenly flesh”; he said “heavenly and earthly bodies.” For every flesh is also a body, but not every body is also flesh. First, among these earthly things, wood is a body but not flesh; but a human being or a cow is both body and flesh. In heavenly things, however, there is no flesh, but simple and bright bodies, which the apostle calls spiritual, though some call them ethereal. And so what he says does not contradict the resurrection of the body: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Rather, he foretells what that which is now flesh and blood will become. Anyone who does not believe that this flesh can be changed into such a nature should be led to faith by steps. If you ask him whether earth can be turned into water, because of their nearness it does not seem incredible to him. Again, if you ask whether water can become air, he answers that this is not absurd either, for they are close to each other. And if you ask about air, whether it can be changed into an ethereal body, that is, a heavenly one, the very nearness persuades him. So what he grants can happen through these steps—that earth is turned into an ethereal body—why does he not believe that, when God’s will is added, by which a human body was able to walk on the waters, it can happen most swiftly, as it is said, “in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Corinthians 15:52), without any such steps, just as smoke is often turned into flame with marvelous speed? For our flesh is certainly from earth. Yet the philosophers, whose arguments are often used to resist the resurrection of the body, and who assert that no earthly body can exist in heaven, grant that every body can be turned and changed into every body. When this resurrection of the body has taken place, freed from the condition of time, we will fully enjoy eternal life with ineffable love and stability, without corruption. For then what is written will happen: “Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your strife?” (1 Corinthians 15:54–55).

last_rejected.why: angelicae modifies inmutationis, not the reverse; 'angelic transformation/change into angels' is meant, not 'change by angels'.
last_rejected.ruling: Genitive 'inmutationis angelicae' is naturally read as 'angelic change'; ambiguity doesn't make 'angelic change' a major error.

last_rejected.quote: what he says does not contradict the resurrection of the body
last_rejected.source_quote: non carnis resurrectioni contradicit illud, quod ait
last_rejected.why: The antecedent of 'illud, quod ait' is the quotation that follows ('flesh and blood...'); 'what he says' makes it sound like Paul's general teaching, not the specific statement.
last_rejected.fix: what he said does not contradict the resurrection of the body
last_rejected.ruling: 'What he says' immediately precedes the quoted statement; no misleading ambiguity for a careful reader.

last_rejected.why: The subject shifts to the doubter; 'he' should refer to the person being led to faith, not Paul. The Latin asks why the doubter won't believe.
last_rejected.ruling: 'He' throughout clearly refers to the doubter being led to faith; context prevents misreading as Paul.
